It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing a world that seeks to “remodel the way we think about truth” by claiming that the body belongs to the self, and I must ask you with a gentle heart: why do you ask after the boundaries of ownership and the purpose of suffering in this hour? [13, 1330, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by a “spirit of fraud” that suggests you are your own master, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that “history is His story”—a single, cohesive account of God’s glory where “not one human sinner or demonic power will ever succeed in his rebellion” against the King? [1, 13, 20, 1143, 1407, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to offer “spiritual placebos” like the idea that suffering is merely an “administrative anomaly” to be eliminated by human law, we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs our souls by reminding us that “your life is not your own” [1, 11, 15, 28, 544, 1503, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition—echoed by **John MacArthur**—teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the claim of self-ownership is not an intellectual error but evidence of a “rebellious heart” that has “exchanged the truth of God for the lie” (Romans 1:25) [15, 68, 713, 1143, 1340, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Blueprint of Ownership (Creation)**

**Verse**
“So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). [1225, 1236, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Scriptures teach that humanity is the “crowning point of creation,” and the *Imago Dei* defines our “unique relation to God,” setting us “apart from the animals” and all mechanical constructs [1236, 1313, 1322, Conversation History]. Our dignity is not earned by “achievement, insights, and wisdom” but is inherent because “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7) [1227, 1241, 1406, 1531, Conversation History]. Because we are God’s “representative and representation” on the earth, our bodies are designed to “bring glory to Christ,” for “all things were created through Him and for Him” (Colossians 1:16) [543, 544, 1238, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not be deceived” by “worldly philosophies” that suggest your body is a private possession for “self-satisfaction,” for “none of us lives to himself, and no one dies to himself; for if we live, we live for the Lord, or if we die, we die for the Lord” (Romans 14:7–8) [12, 91, 258, 679, 1406, 1502, 1670, Conversation History]. Recognize that “he who trusts in his own heart is a fool,” and you must instead “tremble at My word,” which declares that you exist “to bring glory to God” [7, 11, 79, 91, 1406, 1503, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, “national greatness” was a “temporal sign” of God’s favor, yet the Jews were reminded that “man shall not live by bread alone; but man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3) [409, 1219, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our posture, showing that our “citizenship is in heaven” and we are “sojourners and pilgrims” whose true home is the “heavenly Jerusalem” (Philippians 3:20; Hebrews 12:22) [13, 26, 38, 142, 440, 1116, 1203, 1313, 1320, 1426, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: The Theft of Autonomy (The Fall)**

**Verse**
“ ‘For God knows that in the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil’ ” (Genesis 3:5). [767, 1229, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The “record of history” reveals that the first “imitation” of truth occurred in the Garden when the serpent tempted man to believe he could “be like God” through his own independent choice [762, 767, 1362, 1503, Conversation History]. This was a “wicked deed” where man “turned his back on the voice of God” to follow his own “will and reason,” which had become “utterly corrupt” [291, 1248, 1255, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition—echoed by **Voddie Baucham**—notes that “unbelief is the seed” of this rebellion, leading man to “exchange the truth of God for a lie” (Romans 1:25) [1, 205, 549, 1340, 1388, Conversation History]. As a result, the body is now “incarcerated in fallen humanness,” and “sin is the monarch that rules the heart of every man” (Romans 6:12) [49, 581, 1262, 1365, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not look for some other fountain of knowledge” in “career” or “personal freedom” to satisfy your soul, for “every moving thing that lives shall be food for you,” but your spiritual life depends on the Word of the King (Genesis 9:3) [51, 123, 974, 1406, 1503, Conversation History]. Recognize that “sin misses the mark of God’s standard,” and seeking absolute autonomy only leads to becoming “wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17) [51, 144, 989, 992, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of the Curse**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, “the soul who sins shall die,” and “temporal judgments” like “wasting disease” were used to show that “sin is a disgrace to any people” (Proverbs 14:34; Leviticus 26:16) [14, 641, 736, 1147, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** the concept of desolation, revealing that while the “form of this world is passing away,” the “Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2) [12, 307, 463, 1005, 1078, 1214, 1684, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: The Price of Possession (Redemption)**

**Verse**
“Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? For you were bought at a price; therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). [573, 668, 843, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Reformed theology—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that “true Christianity is not about adding Jesus to my life,” but about acknowledging that we have been “purchased by Christ through His death on the cross” [232, 244, 304, 314, Conversation History]. We have been “transformed from slaves of sin into the sons and daughters of righteousness,” and our “self-identity is found in our allegiance to the King of kings” (Romans 6:17–18) [244, 315, 343, 361, Conversation History]. Because we are “fellow-slaves” who “belong to the one Master,” our “sole objective” is to “present [our] bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God” (Romans 12:1) [34, 101, 245, 308, 381, 387, 611, 1444, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Your life is not your own,” and you must “discipline your body and bring it into subjection,” for “He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6; 1 Corinthians 9:27) [5, 11, 13, 79, 116, 201, 544, 573, 575, 759, 813, 829, 953, 956, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1515, 1572, 1670, 1709, Conversation History]. Do “not be conformed to this world,” but find “repose of the soul” in being “clothed in the perfect righteousness the law requires” (Romans 12:2) [13, 24, 35, 126, 142, 160, 610, 672, 868, 1445, 1550, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: From Slave to Son**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, “lineage and circumcision” were seen as the marks of the chosen, yet the NT **revises** this by showing that “true circumcision is that of the heart” (Romans 2:29) [147, 1101, 1266, 1352, Conversation History]. We are now “adopted as sons” through the “Spirit of adoption,” giving us the “right to approach God in prayer” and find “childlike assurance” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:4–5) [140, 318, 319, 320, 324, 327, 466, 693, 695, 696, 732, 1076, 1077, 1286, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Altar of Weakness (State, Sovereignty, and Suffering)**

**Verse**
“And He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore most gladly I will rather boast in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). [101, 483, 597, 599, 626, 725, 748, 869, 959, 961, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—echoed by **Paul Washer**—teaches that “suffering is a way for God to display His grace and power,” and it acts as a “verbal cudgel” to “peel away the flesh and drive you to Himself” [63, 268, 485, 599, 748, 774, Conversation History]. When the state claims authority over life and death—treating suffering as a “problem” to be managed—it often “wrote themselves into God’s office,” forgetting that “the judgment is God’s” and the magistrate is but a “minister to you for good” (Deuteronomy 1:17; Romans 13:4) [11, 37, 75, 79, 131, 136, 1025, 1044, 1114, 1185, 1342, 1422, 1473, 1503, 1709, Conversation History]. The church militant knows that “Christ ultimately crushes the kingdoms of men,” and our “victory” is found not in “political maneuvering” but in being “faithful until death” (Revelation 2:10; 11:15) [11, 13, 16, 20, 21, 23, 24, 31, 35, 67, 103, 136, 710, 726, 753, 968, 1113, 1199, 1233, 1259, 1260, 1266, 1268, 1288, 1290, 1300, 1301, 1311, 1315, 1503, 1515, 1519, 1524, 1532, 1636, 1684, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Trade in your worry for trust,” for the Lord “will not let your foot slip,” and “when anxiety was great within me, Your consolation brought joy to my soul” (Psalm 121:3; 94:19) [62, 72, 80, 86, 89, 90, 94, 201, 1033, 1113, 1143, 1166, 1211, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. “Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “perfect justice will come” and He will “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:10) [13, 14, 21, 24, 32, 92, 94, 109, 121, 201, 329, 352, 470, 563, 569, 712, 727, 816, 822, 825, 940, 948, 1132, 1143, 1313, 1315, 1408, 1426, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Civil vs. Divine Decrees**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, God used “hostile nations” as a “rod of My anger,” yet He held them “responsible for their own rejection” of the truth (Isaiah 10:5; Romans 9:22) [66, 650, 731, 866, 917, 1110, 1130, 1133, 1316, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “warfare,” teaching that while we are “subject to the governing authorities” in mundane matters, we must “obey God rather than men” if the state tries to “tamper with or attempt to tone down the gospel” (Acts 5:29; Romans 13:1) [11, 15, 19, 34, 75, 845, 1130, 1143, 1144, 1176, 1184, 1205, 1246, 1247, 1256, 1284, 1300, 1316, 1342, 1422, 1431, 1473, 1500, 1503, 1528, 1529, 1532, 1545, 1636, 1638, 1720, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 73, 87, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 291, 300, 311, 324, 332, 361, 405, 413, 414, 444, 449, 591, 834, 1138, 1407, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

God genuinely “desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” Yet, in “the eternal purpose which He carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Eph. 3:11), He chose only the elect “out of the world” (John 17:6) and passed over the rest, leaving them to the damning consequences of their sin (cf. Rom. 1:18–32). The culpability for their damnation rests entirely on them because of their sin and rejection of God. God is not to blame for their unbelief. Since God “desires all men to be saved,” we are not required to ascertain that a person is elect before praying for that person’s salvation. God alone knows who all the elect are (2 Tim. 2:19). We may pray “on behalf of all men” with full assurance that such prayers are “good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior.” After all, “The LORD is gracious and merciful; slow to anger and great in lovingkindness. The LORD is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works” (Ps. 145:8–9).

Now, this is an Arminian theologian, but he is acknowledging the biblical truth that God not only sovereignly oversees everything that happens in His creation, but He is personally involved at the most intimate level in every development and every process that occurs in the outworking of history. There's nothing that God's not involved in. And nothing that He doesn't control and govern and oversee. And God will triumph completely regardless of what it looks like at any moment. God's purposes will not be thwarted. His plan cannot be derailed.

Not surprisingly, the very notion of such absolute enslavement (a doctrine commonly known as “total depravity” or “total inability”11 ) is repugnant to the fallen human heart. In fact, no doctrine is more hated by unbelievers than this one, and even some Christians find it so offensive that they zealously attack it.12 Though the doctrine of total depravity is often the most attacked and minimized of the doctrines of grace, it is the most distinctly Christian doctrine because it is foundational to a right understanding of the gospel (in which God initiates everything and receives all the glory). The neglect of this doctrine within American evangelicalism has resulted in all kinds of errors, including both the watered-down gospel and the seeker-driven pragmatism of the church growth movement. But the Scripture is clear: unless the Spirit of God gives spiritual life, all sinners are completely unable to change their fallen nature or to rescue themselves from sin and divine judgment. They can neither initiate nor accomplish any aspect of their redemption. Even the supposed “good things” that unbelievers do are like filthy rags before a holy God (Isa. 64:6). Contrast that with every other religious system, in which people are told that through their own efforts they can achieve some level of righteousness, thereby contributing to their salvation. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Of course, those under Satan’s dominion will share his same demise of eternal destruction. Though sin promises satisfaction and life to its slaves, its reward is in actuality the exact opposite—misery in this life and condemnation in the next.20 The astonishing reality is that even if the sinner could change the condition of his heart—which Scripture teaches is impossible (Jer. 13:23)— no unbeliever would ever will to do so. Left to his own natural reason and volition, the unredeemed sinner will always choose slavery to sin over obedience to God. Until the Lord intervenes, the sinner is neither able nor willing to abandon his sin and serve God in righteousness. Both his will and his reason are utterly corrupt. The New Testament builds on the joy and wonder of human adoption by using it as an analogy to describe God’s fatherly love for us. We were spiritual orphans, under the cruel oppression of sin and Satan. As Scripture depicts it, we were “children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3), “sons of disobedience” (Eph. 2:2; 5:6), “slaves of sin” (Rom. 6:17), and the followers of our “father the devil” (John 8:44). We had no home but this world, no guardian but Satan, and no future but hell. Had we been left in that condition, we would have died in our sins and perished eternally. “But God, being rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us, even when we were dead in our transgressions, made us alive together with Christ (by grace you have been saved)” (Eph. 2:4–5). At great cost to Himself, God intervened to rescue us from sin and bring us into fellowship with Him. In that moment, the Judge of the universe declared us righteous, having clothed us in the sinless perfection of Jesus Christ.2 He made us His slaves, brought us into His kingdom, and welcomed us into His family. Such is the miracle of our spiritual adoption.

Believers can therefore be described as those for whom there remains “no condemnation” (Rom. 8:1). They have been sealed with the Holy Spirit, signifying the irrevocable nature of God’s divine guarantee. They are “protected by the power of God” (1 Peter 1:5), such “that He who began a good work in [them] will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:6). That is why Paul could pray for the Thessalonians, “Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass” (1 Thess. 5:23–24; emphasis added). He would echo those same words in his second letter to that same church: “The Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen and protect you from the evil one” (2 Thess. 3:3). Jude similarly concluded his epistle with this triumphant doxology: “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to make you stand in the presence of His glory blameless with great joy, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen” (vv. 24–25; emphasis added).
